title: Verity County Cooperative Extension
description: The county extension office on Herron Road: soil test bags, the applicator recertification date, the 4-H premium book, two tree disease alerts, and which beetle it actually is.

data.author: Ellen Pitzer
data.tagline: Agriculture and natural resources, Verity and Pell counties. Gridfall office open Tuesday and Thursday.
data.about:
The Verity County office of the cooperative extension service. Room 102, County Extension Building, 1447 Herron Road, Gridfall. Open Tuesday and Thursday, 8:30 to 4:00.

I am Ellen Pitzer. Agriculture and natural resources educator since 2011, and since July 2017 the same one position split between Verity and Pell counties, which is one person and two county boards and two sets of everything.

[b]What this office does:[/b] soil and forage test bags and the results after, pesticide applicator training and recertification, crop and pasture questions, tree and shrub problems, the plant clinic table at the Marchfield farmers market on Saturdays June through September, pressure canner dial gauge testing, and the 4-H programme, which is Tammy Rusk's and not mine.

[b]What it does not do:[/b] test water, which is the health department, or settle a fence line, or tell you what your neighbour sprayed.

I post here when there is a date people need or a question I have answered more than about thirty times. The comment box is open. Some of what arrives in it is not written by anybody.

Room 101 in this building is the soil and water conservation district and they have the aerial photographs back to 1949, which is the single most useful drawer in the county and is not mine.

posts.title: Office hours for the rest of the year
posts.body:
The county's appropriation to this office for 2025 is $23,000. In 2023 it was $46,000. The state's share of my salary did not change, so what changed is the days.

Here is what that means at the counter.

[b]Gridfall office, Room 102, County Extension Building, 1447 Herron Road.[/b] Tuesday and Thursday, 8:30 to 4:00. Walk in. You will not get seen faster by making an appointment, because there are no appointments.

Wednesday I am in the Pell County office. Monday and Friday I am in a truck in one of the two counties and the truck does not have a desk in it.

The office telephone forwards to Pell when I am not here. If you leave a message on the Verity number it goes into a box that was set up in 2014 and nobody has the code for it. I have asked twice. [u]Do not leave a message on the Verity number.[/u] Email gets answered in the evening, which is not overtime, it is just when it gets answered.

What does not change: soil test bags, the applicator recertification meeting in the winter, the 4-H program, the plant clinic table at the Marchfield farmers market on Saturdays from June through September, and pressure canner gauge testing.

What does change: I am not driving out to look at one tree. If there are six things on the same road I will come and look at all six.

Ruth Cannady put the county appropriations sheet up alongside her March piece on the budget. The extension line is on page 4 of it if you want to see our number next to the other numbers. [url=synth://thequarry.news/]thequarry.news[/url]

Hal Brenner telephoned about it as well, and asked two questions, and both of them were the right questions, and I gave him the same answer I have given here because it is the only answer there is. [url=synth://brenners-notebook.email/]brenners-notebook.email[/url]

posts.title: Do not prune an oak until the middle of July
posts.body:
[b]15 April to 15 July.[/b] Do not prune, top, cable, climb with spikes, hit with a mower deck, or otherwise open an oak in that window.

The reason is a fungus that is moved from tree to tree by small sap beetles. The beetles are attracted to a fresh wound on an oak within about fifteen minutes of it being made, and they are carrying the fungus off a tree that died last year. In the red oak group, which is your pin oak, red oak and black oak, an infected tree can go from full canopy to bare in one summer. The white oak group is slower and sometimes survives it.

If a storm takes a limb in June, you do not have a choice. Paint the wound. That is the one case in modern tree care where wound paint is the right answer, and I know what you have read about wound paint, and this is the exception.

It also moves underground. Oaks of the same species within about fifty feet of each other graft their roots together, and the fungus travels through the graft. That is why oak wilt shows up as a ring of dead trees on a fence line and not as one tree in the middle of a lawn.

Two more things.

[list][*]Do not cut a dead oak up for firewood and give it away. Bark-on oak that died last summer is exactly the thing the beetles come to.
[*]An oak with brown leaf edges in August is almost never oak wilt. That is scorch, and scorch is a water problem, and the water problem is usually that the tree is in a lawn that gets twenty minutes of sprinkler three times a week, which is worse than nothing.
[/list]

Brush you are getting rid of: the burn permit is on the county portal and it is free, and it takes about four minutes. [url=synth://verity.county.gov/s/burn-permit]verity.county.gov[/url]. If it is windy, the fire department would rather you called them first than called them second. [url=synth://ashkettlevfd.org/]ashkettlevfd.org[/url]

posts.title: Bring me your dial gauge
posts.body:
Pressure canner gauge testing is free and takes about ten minutes. Any Tuesday or Thursday I am here.

[b]Bring the lid only.[/b] Not the whole canner. I do not need twenty-two pounds of aluminium on the counter and neither do you.

Two kinds of gauge. A [i]dial[/i] gauge has a needle and a face and it drifts, and it needs testing every year. A [i]weighted[/i] gauge is the piece that rocks or jiggles, and it does not drift and cannot be tested. What a weighted gauge needs is the vent pipe held up to a window to see daylight through it, which you can do yourself right now.

If a dial gauge reads more than two pounds off, replace the gauge. A gauge is about $25 and a replacement lid gasket while you are at it is about $12. Last year I tested 31 gauges. Five were off. Two were off by more than four pounds and both of those were the same make and both had been in a cupboard since somebody's mother died.

A gauge reading two pounds low means you have been under-processing for however long it has been drifting. Nobody has got sick from it that I know of. That is not the same as it being fine.

The other half of this: I cannot tell you your grandmother's recipe is safe. I can tell you what the tested process for that food is, and the two are not always the same thing, and I am not going to argue with you about your grandmother. Tomatoes have changed. The recommendation changed in 1994 and again in 2015 and the reason both times was acidity, not fashion.

Nothing low-acid in a water bath. Green beans, corn, carrots, soup, anything with meat in it: pressure or freeze it. That is the whole rule and the rest is detail.

posts.title: First cutting
posts.body:
Everybody's first cutting is stemmy and nobody wants to hear why, so I will put it here where it can be ignored quietly.

There were nineteen days between the first stretch of three dry days and the second one. Most of this county cut in the second stretch. Grass that stood through the 20th of June is grass that made a seed head, and a seed head is stem, and stem is where the digestibility goes.

That is not a criticism. You cut when the weather let you cut. I am writing down what the bale is so you feed it knowing.

[b]Moisture.[/b] Small squares under 20 percent. Large rounds under 16, or wrap them. A round bale put up at 22 percent will heat, and a bale that heats loses protein you paid for in fertiliser, and in a bad case it does not stop heating.

[b]Test it.[/b] A forage sample through the same state lab is $22 and comes back in about a week. A core sampler is a $200 tool and there is one in this office that anybody may borrow, along with a drill, and I would rather lend it out than own it.

What the test is for: a dry beef cow in the middle third does not need what a growing heifer needs, and if you know which bales are the stemmy ones you can feed them to the cows that can take it and stop buying supplement for the whole herd. That decision is worth more than the $22 about forty times over and it is the single most common thing I get told is not worth doing.

Second cutting will be better. It always is, and it is always less of it.

posts.title: Four things people bring me that are not a disease, and one that is
posts.body:
[b]1. The maple that is thin on one side.[/b] It is not a disease. It is a girdling root, and the girdling root is there because the tree was planted too deep, and it was planted too deep in about 2009 when everybody in this county put in a maple. Dig at the base. If you cannot find the flare where the trunk turns into roots, the flare is under the soil, and it has been under the soil for sixteen years. Sometimes you can cut the root. Often you are sixteen years late.

While we are here: the mulch is not supposed to touch the trunk. Three inches deep, pulled back a hand's width. A mulch volcano keeps the bark wet and the bark rots and then the tree is doing the same thing the girdling root does, only faster.

[b]2. The birch with neat rows of holes.[/b] Sapsucker. A bird. The holes are in tidy horizontal lines because the bird is farming sap and comes back to the same tree. It is not a borer and it does not kill the tree except in the rare case where a bird rings it all the way round. There is nothing to spray at a woodpecker.

[b]3. The brown rings in the lawn.[/b] Two candidates, and you know which one you have. Dark green ring with dead middle is a dog. Straw-coloured everywhere with green along the hose run is drought, and cool-season grass going dormant in July is grass doing its job, not grass dying. It comes back in September. It always comes back in September.

[b]4. The tomato with the black bottom.[/b] Blossom end rot. Not a fungus and not a bug. Calcium that did not get to the fruit, and it did not get there because the watering was uneven, and it is nearly never because your soil is short of calcium. If your soil test says the calcium is fine, and around here it is fine, then do not put a shell or a tablet in the hole. Water the same amount on the same days and mulch it.

[b]And the one that is a disease.[/b] Blue spruce with the bottom third bare and the needles going purple-brown and dropping from the inside out is Rhizosphaera needle cast. That is a fungus and I can tell you about a three-year fungicide programme, correctly timed twice each spring, that costs more than the tree and will not bring back a branch that is already bare. Your spruce is thirty-one years old. It is a Colorado tree, in a county that is humid in June, and this is what happens to it here at about thirty. I am not going to pretend otherwise so that you feel better about the money.

Plant something else next time. There is a list at the office and it is one page.

posts.title: Wells are the health department, and here is the number
posts.body:
I do not test water. This office has not tested water since the person who did it retired in 2006, and I still get four calls a month about it, so here it is in writing.

Private well testing is the county health department. Free coliform and nitrate sample kits in the autumn, and the bottle has to be back at the lab within a set number of hours, which is why they only hand them out on particular days. [url=synth://verityhealth.gov/s/well-water]verityhealth.gov[/url] has the dates and the drop times. The county portal has the same page with an older phone number on it. [url=synth://verity.county.gov/s/well-water]verity.county.gov[/url]

Two things worth knowing while you are down there.

[b]Nitrate is the one to actually worry about[/b], and only in particular situations: a shallow well, a dug well, a well downhill of a barnyard or a feedlot, and a house with an infant under six months in it. If any of those describe you, test for nitrate whether or not you think anything is wrong. Nitrate does not smell, taste or look like anything.

[b]A water softener is not a treatment for nitrate.[/b] It is not a treatment for bacteria either. It takes hardness out. That is all it does. I have had three people tell me their softener handles it, and all three had been sold that by the same kind of person.

If your test comes back with coliform, it is usually the well cap or the casing seal, and it is usually fixable in an afternoon for the price of a cap. Do not start with shock chlorination and skip the part where you find out why.

What I will do is read the result with you and tell you what the numbers mean. Bring the sheet.

posts.title: How to take a soil sample so the number means something
posts.body:
Autumn is the right time and almost nobody does it then. The lab is quiet, lime has all winter to react, and there is still a spreader available. In May the lab is three weeks out and the lime you spread in May is doing nothing for the crop you planted in April.

[b]The tool.[/b] A soil probe. There are two in this office that anybody may borrow and the coop at Marchfield has two more. [url=synth://marchfield-coop.com/]marchfield-coop.com[/url], which has not been touched since 2014, but the elevator is open and Corinne knows where the probes are. A clean spade works if you cut a thin slice and not a wedge.

[b]The depth.[/b] Six to eight inches for tilled ground. Three to four inches for a lawn, a pasture, or no-till. Pick one and be consistent, because pH and phosphorus both stratify and a four-inch sample and an eight-inch sample off the same field are two different fields.

[b]The cores.[/b] Fifteen to twenty per sample. Walk a zigzag across the area and take one every so many paces without looking at where you are putting the probe, because if you look you will avoid the bad spots or you will only hit them.

A sample is fifteen to twenty cores mixed together. A sample is not one shovelful out of the place where nothing grows. I get that one about twice a month and the number that comes back is true and useless.

[b]The bucket.[/b] Plastic. Not galvanised, because galvanised is zinc and zinc is one of the things on the sheet. Mix the cores until it is one colour, then fill the bag to the line.

[b]The label.[/b] Write something on the bag you will recognise in three years. "Garden" is not that. "Garden, east of the drive" is.

[b]How many.[/b] One sample per field, or per part of a field that is obviously different ground, or per problem area kept separate from the rest. Not one for the whole farm and not one per acre.

[b]The cost.[/b] $18 a sample, cheque made out to the lab, bags and forms in the rack in the hallway outside Room 102. I put the box in the post on Tuesdays. Results come back to you and to me, and mine goes in a folder so that when you call in March I can find it.

[b]What you get.[/b] pH, buffer pH, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium, organic matter, cation exchange capacity. No nitrogen, and you do not want nitrogen on it, because a nitrate number off a bag of soil mailed in October tells you what happened in October.

[b]Reading it.[/b] Three things do most of the work.

[list][*]pH. Corn and beans want about 6.2. Alfalfa wants 6.5 and will not forgive you for 5.8. The buffer pH is the one that says how much lime it takes to move it, and that is the number the recommendation comes off, not the pH itself.
[*]Phosphorus. If it comes back in the thirties on row crop ground, that is plenty. Every second garden sample in this county comes back over 150 because somebody has been putting chicken manure on it for eleven years. If yours says 210 you do not need phosphorus and you have not needed it since about 2016, and the general purpose fertiliser you are buying is a third phosphorus.
[*]Organic matter. It moves slowly and it is the only number on the sheet you cannot buy. Watch it across ten years, not across two.
[/list]

[b]The crop code.[/b] The recommendation is written for whatever you put in that box. If you write lawn and you meant vegetable garden, the sheet you get back is a lawn recommendation and it is not wrong, it is answering the question you asked.

posts.title: Master Gardener class, January to March
posts.body:
Twelve Tuesday evenings, 6 January to 24 March, 6:30 to 9:00, Room 104. Twelve seats.

$175. That covers the manual, which is 640 pages in a binder and is the only part of the course you keep. It does not cover the coffee, which is free and is not good.

What the evenings are: botany, soils, plant nutrition, entomology, plant pathology, weed identification, woody ornamentals, vegetables, fruit, lawns, pesticide safety, and one night that is nothing but diagnostics, which is looking at a sick plant and working backwards, and which is the only night people talk about afterwards.

The commitment is thirty volunteer hours in the first year. That is the plant clinic table at the Marchfield market on Saturdays, the demonstration beds at the fairgrounds, the seed library at the library, and two hours a month answering the office telephone on Tuesdays, which sounds like the worst of them and is the one people fight over.

You do not need to know anything to start. Half of what people arrive knowing is wrong and a fair bit of the course is about that, gently.

Last year eleven started and nine finished. The two who stopped both had Tuesday work, which I could not do anything about.

Ring or email. First twelve, and if there are more than twelve I will run a list and hold it for next year, and I have never yet had to.

[b]Not the second Tuesday.[/b] The astronomy club has Room 104 on the second Tuesday of the month and has had it since 1978, and we work around them, and if you think I am going to be the one to move them you have not met them. [url=synth://stargazers.verity.net/]stargazers.verity.net[/url]

The diagnostics night does not work online, because the whole point of it is that somebody hands you a bag with a dead branch in it and will not tell you anything else. Do the online one if the drive is the difference between doing it and not.

posts.title: Private applicator recertification is Thursday 5 February
posts.body:
[b]Thursday 5 February, 9:00 to 12:00, Room 104, County Extension Building, 1447 Herron Road.[/b] Doors and coffee at 8:30.

Three credit hours, which is what a private applicator licence needs for the cycle that ends this year. Sign the sheet when you come in and sign it again when you leave, because the state wants both and if you leave at 11:15 I cannot give you the three hours no matter how well I know you.

[b]$35, cheque or money order, made out to the state.[/b] I cannot take a card and I cannot take cash. That is not my rule, I have asked about it twice, and the answer both times was that the office does not hold funds.

[b]Bring your licence number.[/b] Every single year, four people arrive without it, and the state's lookup is down about as often as it is up. Write it on a card and put the card in the truck.

What we are covering:

[list][*]Label reading. We will go through one label, all of it, out loud, and the room will get restless in the middle and that is the part where the rotation restrictions are.
[*]The state's 2025 changes to the dicamba application cut-off dates. Read them before you buy, not after.
[*]Drift. Nozzle selection and boom height, with the demonstration rig in the parking lot if it is above freezing, and in the room with slides if it is not.
[*]Record keeping. It is the part everybody fails an inspection on and it is the part everybody thinks they have covered. Forty-eight hours, in writing, and "in writing" does not mean in your head until the weekend.
[/list]

[b]This meeting does not cover commercial applicators.[/b] If you are 3A or 6, the regional is in Pell on Tuesday 3 February and it is a different fee and a different sign-in. Do not come here and then find out at 12:01.

[b]Testing.[/b] The state proctors the private applicator exam at this office on the third Wednesday of the month. Register two weeks ahead. $30 for the exam, $45 for the licence, photo identification, and a pencil, and I will not be in the room.

One correction in advance. The county's answer machine is telling people this meeting is in March. It is not in March and it has not been in March since 2019. [url=synth://ask.verity.ai/]ask.verity.ai[/url] tells people the same thing, and I have no way to correct it, and I have stopped trying.

posts.title: The beetles coming out of your firewood
posts.body:
Seven people in nine days. All seven brought me the same insect and six of them asked the same question, which is whether it is the emerald ash borer.

It is not. In every one of the seven cases it was a redheaded ash borer, which is a native longhorned beetle, which came out of firewood that had been stacked in a warm room for a week.

Short version:

[list][*]The emerald ash borer does not fly in January in this county. Not once, not in a mild winter, not ever. Adults are out from late May to about the first of August.
[*]What you have is reddish brown with four pale bands across its back and antennae about half as long as it is. The emerald ash borer is metallic green and half an inch and its antennae are short.
[*]It came out of wood that was already dead when you split it. It cannot start in a living tree, it cannot get into your house framing, and it will not come back to the same wood.
[*]It will keep happening for as long as the stack is by the stove. Put the wood outside and bring in what you will burn that day.
[/list]

By my own count I have now answered this more than four hundred times since August 2019, in the office, on the telephone, twice in a car park and once at a funeral. It is the same three insects every time and one of them is a moth.

So in the spring I am going to write the whole thing out properly, with what to look at and in what order, and then I am going to send people the link, and that will be that.

posts.title: Frost seeding clover
posts.body:
Late February into the first week of March, on a morning when the ground is still hard enough to walk on without printing it.

Two to four pounds of red clover per acre broadcast on frozen ground. The freeze and thaw opens the soil and closes it again over the seed, and that is the whole mechanism. It costs about $14 an acre and it works about three years in four.

What makes it fail:

[list][*]A thatch of old grass. The seed has to reach dirt. Graze it or clip it hard in the autumn so there is something to fall into.
[*]Going too late. Once the ground stops freezing at night you are broadcasting seed onto a lawn.
[*]Trying it with grass seed. Orchardgrass and fescue mostly do not take this way. Clover does because the seed is small and hard and round and gets into a crack.
[*]A residual herbicide from last year. Read the rotation restriction on the label of whatever you sprayed. This is the same thing I say at the recert meeting every February and it is the same label.
[/list]

Why bother: clover fixes its own nitrogen, and on a pasture that has been getting nothing for six years it will do more for the grass than a bag of urea would, and it will do it for three or four years. It also bloats cattle, so if you are putting a lot in, know that going in and manage it.

I have seed sources on one sheet at the office. It is not a recommendation of anybody, it is a list, and two of them are out of county.

posts.body:
Soil test bags are in the rack in the hallway. Take what you need and take a form for each bag.

The lab quotes seven working days and is running nine to eleven. That is the lab, not the post. If you want a result before you buy fertiliser, that is two weeks from the Tuesday I post the box, and the Tuesdays are the 17th, the 24th and the 31st.

[b]$18 a sample now, $20 from 1 July.[/b] First rise since 2022.

The how-to is here and it has not changed: [url=/post/soil-sample-how-to]how to take a soil sample[/url]. The short version is fifteen to twenty cores, one bucket, six to eight inches, and write something useful on the bag.

One other thing. A website that produces county guides at volume has copied most of that post of mine, run it through something, and published it with a $79 four-in-one meter recommended twice in the middle of it. [url=synth://countyfacts.info/]countyfacts.info[/url], if you want to see it.

The meter reads electrical conductivity and reports the result as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. It is not measuring nitrogen, phosphorus or potassium. It cannot. There is no probe at that price that does, and the three numbers it gives you move when the soil is wet.

The same rewrite turned up on a news site with a local name on it, [url=synth://veritycountytoday.com/]veritycountytoday.com[/url], and was then submitted to [url=synth://gridline.social/board/b-local]Gridline[/url] twice in one morning by two accounts, and both submissions have four comments and all eight comments are from the other one.

I do not particularly mind the copying. I mind that the version with my name nowhere on it is the one that comes up first.

posts.title: Oak wilt confirmed, four trees, Nye Mills township
posts.body:
The state plant lab confirmed oak wilt on 6 April in four red oaks on a fence line in Nye Mills township, about a mile north of the fairgrounds. I took the samples on 27 March off the two trees that went bare last July.

This is the second confirmed site in Verity County. The first was in 2021, off Ostrander Road, three trees, and that one has not moved since the trenching.

[b]What is being done.[/b] The landowner is cutting all four and grinding the stumps before 1 May, at his own cost, and he did not have to and did not argue about it. The wood is staying on the property and being covered until it is split and dry.

[b]Trenching.[/b] Red oaks within about fifty feet of each other graft their roots together and the fungus travels through the graft, so cutting the sick tree without cutting the connection moves the problem instead of stopping it. The trench goes five feet deep at a fifty-foot radius beyond the last symptomatic tree. It is expensive. On a fence line with a field on one side it is straightforward, and that is most of why I think this one stays put.

[b]What everybody else should do.[/b]

[list][*]Do not prune, wound or climb an oak between 15 April and 15 July. We are inside that window as of this week.
[*]Do not move oak wood with the bark on. Split, stacked and through one full summer, it is not a risk. A round with bark on it, in June, is.
[*]If an oak drops its leaves from the top down in June or July, with the leaves going dull green to bronze from the tip back and half of them still on the tree when they fall, telephone me. Do not wait for the autumn.
[/list]

I will come and look at an oak. That one I will make the drive for.

The state keeps a list of certified arborists. It is online, I will print you a copy, and there are four on it with a Verity County address and two of those are the same firm.

posts.title: The two ash borers
posts.body:
I said in January that I would write this out and send people the link instead of saying it again. This is it. If you emailed me about a beetle and got a link, this is why.

There are at least three insects in this county that somebody calls the ash borer. One of them is killing every ash we have. The other two turn up in your kitchen and frighten you and are not doing anything. Telling them apart takes about fifteen seconds once you know what to look at, and almost nobody has been told what to look at.

[b]1. Emerald ash borer[/b]

[i]Agrilus planipennis.[/i] The one that matters.

Half an inch long, narrow, bright metallic green, flat across the back, with short antennae. If you can get a wing cover up, the abdomen underneath is coppery red. It is not native. It arrived in this country in the 1990s and it was confirmed in Verity County on 13 August 2019, off a street ash on Ellery Street in Gridfall. I posted the sample on the 6th. I knew what it was when I put it in the envelope and I posted it anyway because a county detection is not a county detection until the state lab says so.

What it does: the adult chews a little notch out of a leaf and does no real harm. The larva is the problem. It feeds in the phloem, just under the bark, in a flat S-shaped gallery packed tight with sawdust the texture of face powder. Enough larvae and the galleries cross, and when they cross the tree cannot move water past them, and it dies from the top down over two to four years.

Signs, in the order you actually get them:

[list][*][b]Canopy thinning at the top.[/b] Nobody notices this. It looks like a hard summer.
[*][b]Blonding.[/b] Woodpeckers work the upper trunk and the big limbs and flake the grey outer bark off in patches, and the patches are pale, and the tree looks like it has been sanded fifteen feet up. This is the sign most people finally see, and in this county they usually see it in February, because there are no leaves in the way.
[*][b]Sprouts.[/b] Thin shoots coming straight out of the trunk and around the base. That is the tree trying everything it has.
[*][b]D-shaped exit holes.[/b] One eighth of an inch, flat on one side, a capital D lying on its back. These come last and they mean the beetles have already left.
[/list]

Flight: late May through to about the first week of August, heaviest the second and third weeks of June. Which is now, as I write this. A beetle indoors in January is not this insect, and that is not a judgement call, it is a calendar.

Where we are with it. Every untreated ash over about eight inches in Gridfall is dead or going. The street trees went first, because they were all one species planted in one decade, and the reason they were all one species is that the elms had gone in the 1960s and ash was what everybody planted next. The woodlot ash in the north of the county are going now. On the branch trail there is a three-quarter-mile stretch between mile 4 and mile 5 where nearly every standing dead tree is an ash, and the parks department has marked what it can reach.

[b]2. Redheaded ash borer[/b]

[i]Neoclytus acuminatus.[/i] Native. A longhorned beetle, which is a completely different family, and if you have one in a jar you can see that in a second: the antennae are half the length of the body and it walks in fast jerks and stops, like a wasp working a windowsill.

Half an inch to three quarters, reddish brown, with four pale yellow bands running across the wing covers, and long reddish legs.

It breeds in wood that is already dead or dying. A tree cut last winter, a limb the ice took, a stack of split ash under a tarp. The exit hole is round. It cannot attack a healthy standing tree, it cannot get into your house framing, it cannot get into furniture, and it will not reinfest wood it has come out of.

You see it in January and February because you brought its wood inside and put it next to a stove and told it that it was spring.

There is also a [b]banded ash borer[/b], [i]Neoclytus caprea[/i], which is the same family, the same habit and the same harmlessness, with greyish-white bands instead of yellow and a slightly later emergence. If you cannot tell those two apart, it does not matter. The answer is the same for both, and the answer is nothing.

[b]3. The one that is a moth[/b]

[i]Podosesia syringae[/i], the lilac borer or ash borer depending on which book you have. It is a clearwing moth and it is a good enough wasp mimic that people kill it in a panic.

The larvae tunnel in the lower trunk, mostly the bottom four feet, of young ash and of lilac, and they prefer a tree that is already stressed, in a lawn, mown into, staked too long. The hole is round, about a quarter inch, with coarse sawdust around it, and very often a papery brown pupal case sticking half out of the hole. That case is the only sign in this entire post you can identify from twenty feet away and be right.

Adults are out in April and May. It is treatable with a bark spray if the timing is right, and the timing comes off pheromone trap catch, and nobody in this county is running those traps, so in practice the timing is the middle of April.

[b]How to tell in fifteen seconds[/b]

[list][*][b]Hole shape.[/b] D-shaped is emerald ash borer and nothing else. Round is everything else in this post.
[*][b]Where on the tree.[/b] High up, all over, with blonding: emerald. Bottom four feet with sawdust and a pupal case: the moth. Wherever the wood was cut or broken: redheaded or banded.
[*][b]When you found it.[/b] Indoors, January to March: redheaded or banded, out of your firewood. Outdoors in June: emerald. April to May and it looks like a wasp: the moth.
[*][b]Was the tree healthy first?[/b] The emerald ash borer kills healthy ash. The other two do not start on a healthy tree. They finish one that is already going, which is why finding them on a tree means looking for what was wrong before they got there.
[/list]

[b]How to send me one[/b]

Pill bottle. Freezer overnight. Bring it in or post it, with three things written down: the date, the town, and whether it came out of the wall, the wood or the tree. That is all I need and I will get back to you the same week.

A photograph of a beetle on a screen door at night, taken with a flash from four feet away, tells me that you have a beetle. I have received about ninety of those and I have identified two.

[b]Treatment, honestly[/b]

Trunk injection with emamectin benzoate, done by a licensed applicator, works. It really does work, which is the part people do not believe until they see an untreated row and a treated one side by side. It runs about $9 to $12 an inch of trunk diameter here and it is good for two to three years, and then you do it again, and you keep doing it for as long as you want the tree.

The soil drench you can buy yourself, imidacloprid, works reasonably on a small tree in decent ground and poorly on a big one, because the tree has to pull it up and a struggling tree is not pulling much of anything. Do not put it down under a tree that is in flower, and do not put it anywhere it runs to a drain.

[b]When not to treat.[/b] If more than about a third of the canopy is gone, you are paying to slow down a dead tree. I say that to people and they do not like it, and then two years later they tell me I was right, and I would rather have been wrong.

Do the arithmetic before the feelings get involved. A 24-inch ash treated every other year from now to 2046 is somewhere around $2,400 in today's money. Taking the same tree down when it is dead and brittle and standing over a driveway is $1,400 to $2,200, and that number goes up every year it stands, because every year it is more dangerous to climb.

A treated tree is worth it when it is a good tree in a place a tree cannot easily be replaced. Four of them in a row along a fence line is a hobby.

[b]Firewood[/b]

Do not move it. Buy it where you burn it. The state's rule is 50 miles; the real rule is your own road.

Dead ash is good firewood and it stands there seasoning itself, and that is exactly the trap. After about the third year dead, an ash is the most dangerous tree on your property to fell. The roots go, the top goes brittle, and it comes apart in the air on the way down instead of falling in one piece. Two people in this county have been hurt doing it since 2022 and both of them had cut a hundred trees before.

If you are going to do it yourself, chaps, a helmet with a screen, and somebody else in the yard who is watching and not helping. The farm store stocks all of that and it is cheaper than the emergency room. [url=synth://countysupply.store/p/p-09]chaps[/url], and the rest of the woodlot shelf is [url=synth://countysupply.store/c/c-saw]here[/url].

[b]Planting back[/b]

Not all one thing. That is the whole lesson of the elms and then the ash and we have now had it twice in sixty years.

Hackberry, swamp white oak, Kentucky coffeetree, and sycamore where there is actually room for a sycamore, which is almost nowhere anybody wants to put one. Not Bradford pear. Not five of anything in a row.

[b]Last[/b]

This county is going to look different for the rest of my working life and nothing in this post changes that. What is in this post is how to tell whether the beetle in your hand is the one doing it, which is the question I actually get asked, and the answer is almost always no.

posts.title: The dead ash on your road frontage is yours
posts.body:
This comes up every autumn and it came up eleven times in August, so here is the plain version.

[b]Who owns the tree.[/b] If the trunk stands outside the road right of way, it is the landowner's tree and the landowner's problem. The right of way on most county roads here is 33 feet from centre line, which on a two-lane road puts the edge somewhere around your ditch and not at your fence. If you are not sure, the land records will tell you. [url=synth://verity.county.gov/s/land-records]verity.county.gov[/url]

The county cuts what is in the right of way when it gets to it. On a township road, "when it gets to it" is not this year. That is not the highway department being difficult, it is two crews and a great many miles, and if you want to hear about it from them rather than from me, the road contact is set out about as clearly as anyone has managed here: [url=synth://askverity.com/q/q-14]askverity.com[/url]

[b]The utility is doing its own thing.[/b] Verity Valley has line clearance crews on the three-phase along Kestrel Road and Ostrander Road this autumn and they are taking ash. Their scope is the wire. They will not take the one in your yard and they are not supposed to. [url=synth://vvpl.news/]vvpl.news[/url]

[b]The trail.[/b] Parks has about forty hazard trees marked between mile 4 and mile 6 and has posted two short closures to get at them. The conditions thread is the only place that gets updated. [url=synth://trailusers.verity.net/topic/tt-03]trailusers.verity.net[/url]

[b]Getting it done.[/b] Three services work in this county and two of them are booked past the new year. Get on a list. Ads turn up in the classifieds every autumn and some of them are people and some of them are a phone number in another state that subcontracts to whoever answers. [url=synth://classifieds.verity.net/c/k-services]classifieds.verity.net[/url]

[b]The wood.[/b] If you are selling it, say in the advert that it is ash and say where it is, because the people who care will care about both. Ronnie types those up by hand over at [url=synth://gridfall-buysell.net/]gridfall-buysell.net[/url] and he will put the town in for you if you forget.

Ask for the certificate of insurance. Then telephone the number printed on the certificate and ask whether the policy is current. A man with a chipper and no certificate who wants cash and started work on your neighbour's tree this morning is a man whose injuries become your problem.

Which insect it is, and why the one that came out of your firewood in January is not the one that killed the tree, is written out here: [url=/post/two-ash-borers]the two ash borers[/url].

[b]And.[/b] An ash that has been dead three years is not a tree any more. It is a column of dry wood standing up out of habit. Do not lean a ladder on it, do not tie anything to it, do not let a child climb it, and do not go up it with a saw because you have taken down twenty other trees.

posts.title: Sample this month, and the office in October
posts.body:
Bags are in the rack. $20 a sample now. The lab is back to nine days and the box goes in the post on Tuesdays.

Do it this month. Lime wants the winter to work and there is still a spreader to be had in October. If you wait until April you will be behind everyone else who waited until April and the answer will arrive after you have already bought the fertiliser.

[b]The office will be dark on the 6th and 7th of October.[/b] State in-service, two days, and the Pell number will be on the door and on the recording that actually plays.

The plant clinic table at the market is finished for the year. 61 samples over the summer. 22 of them were a tree planted too deep, which is exactly the number it was last year, which either says something about this county or about me.

One other thing, because somebody asked twice. I was at the pull-off at the quarry cut on Tuesday afternoon, and no, I was not out there listening to anything. I was counting dead ash on the south face with a pair of binoculars at about four o'clock and I left before the light went. There are 34 standing dead in the view from that pull-off and 11 of them are within falling distance of where people park, and I have put that in writing to the parks department, who will put it on a list.

Apparently mine is the only white truck in the county.
